cur.100.algorithm:
y′ = f(x)g(y) と書く。
分離する: dy/g(y) = f(x) dx。
両辺を積分し、定数を1つ加える。
可能なら y について解く。不可能なら陰関数の関係のまま残す。
定数解 g(y) = 0 を加え、初期条件を適用する。
cur.100.answer: 分離すると dy/y = 4x/(x² + 1) dx となる。積分すると ln|y| = 2 ln(x² + 1) + C、よって y = C(x² + 1)²。
cur.100.idea: 変数分離形は x の関数と y の関数の積に因数分解できる。y を含む項をすべて一方に、x を含む項をすべて他方に移すと、問題は2つの積分に帰着する。
cur.100.pitfall: g(y) で割ると平衡解 g(y) = 0 が失われる。これらは別に列挙する。
cur.100.theory.0: Separation means keeping each variable with its own differential: $\frac{dy}{g(y)}=f(x)\,dx$. Integrating both sides gives a relation between $y$ and $x$ that need not be explicit; that is why the answer is sometimes kept in the implicit form $F(x,y)=C$.
cur.100.theory.1: The subtle point is dividing by $g(y)$. If $g(y_0)=0$, the constant function $y=y_0$ is also a solution and is lost by the division. These equilibrium solutions must be checked separately; sometimes the initial condition sits exactly on one of them.
cur.101.algorithm:
方程式を M(x,y) dx + N(x,y) dy = 0 と書く。
M_y = N_x を確かめる。
完全なら M を x について積分し、F_y を N と比較して y の未知関数を求める。
F(x,y) = C とおく。
完全でなければ μ(x) = exp(∫(M_y − N_x)/N dx) または同様の μ(y) を試す。
cur.101.answer: M_y = 1 = N_x なので完全形である。積分すると F = x² + xy + y² となり、解は x² + xy + y² = C。
cur.101.idea: 完全形はポテンシャル関数 F(x,y) の微分である。解はレベル曲線 F(x,y) = C であり、完全性は偏導関数の交差検定で判定する。
cur.101.pitfall: 完全性の判定は M_y = N_x であり、M_x = N_y ではない。偏導関数を取り違えるのがよくある誤りである。
cur.101.theory.0: If $F$ exists, $dF=F_x\,dx+F_y\,dy$, so $F_x=M$ and $F_y=N$. The equality of mixed partials $F_{xy}=F_{yx}$ gives $M_y=N_x$. Integrating $M$ with respect to $x$ determines $F$ up to an unknown function of $y$, which is found by comparison with $N$.
cur.101.theory.1: If the condition fails, an integrating factor $\mu(x)$ or $\mu(y)$ sometimes makes the equation exact. Such a factor is not guaranteed to exist, but when it depends on a single variable it is found from a simple differential equation.
cur.102.algorithm:
(x,y) を (tx,ty) に置き換えても f が変わらないことを確かめる。すなわち y′ = f(y/x)。
y = vx と y′ = v + xv′ を代入する。
x dv/dx = f(v) − v に整理する。
分離して積分する: ∫dv/(f(v) − v) = ∫dx/x。
v = y/x に戻し、f(v) − v = 0 の解があれば加える。
cur.102.answer: y = vx とすると y′ = v + xv′ で、方程式は xv′ = 1/v となる。よって v² = 2 ln|x| + C、y² = x²(2 ln|x| + C)。
cur.102.idea: 同次形の1階方程式は、x と y に比 y/x を通してのみ依存する。y = vx と置くと、v と x に関する変数分離形になる。
cur.102.pitfall: 同次性を確かめる前に y = vx を使ってはならない。平行移動した方程式には1次式の置換が必要である。
cur.102.theory.0: The word "homogeneous" here is not the same as for a linear equation. It means $f(x,y)$ is unchanged by scaling both variables together: $f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)$. Such a function can be written as a function of the ratio $y/x$, and that ratio is the key to the solution.
cur.102.theory.1: With $y=vx$ and the product rule, $y'=v+xv'$. Substituting into $v+xv'=f(v)$ gives $x\frac{dv}{dx}=f(v)-v$, which is separable. After integrating, replace $v$ by $y/x$. Constant solutions satisfying $f(v)-v=0$ must also be checked separately.
cur.103.algorithm:
y′ + P(x)y = Q(x)yⁿ と書く。
yⁿ で割る。
v = y^(1−n) と置くと、v′ = (1−n)y^(−n)y′。
得られた線形方程式を v について解く。
元に戻し、n > 0 のとき y = 0 を加える。
cur.103.answer: y′ − y = y² と書き直すと n = 2、v = y⁻¹。すると v′ + v = −1、v = Ce⁻ˣ − 1、y = 1/(Ce⁻ˣ − 1)。
cur.103.idea: ベルヌーイ方程式は、右辺の y のべきを除けば線形である。v = y^(1−n) と置くとそのべきが消え、線形方程式が得られる。
cur.103.pitfall: n = 0 と n = 1 は線形方程式でありベルヌーイではない。直接解く。
cur.103.theory.0: For $n\neq 0,1$ the equation is nonlinear, but dividing by $y^n$ and setting $v=y^{1-n}$ linearises it. Since $v'=(1-n)y^{-n}y'$, the equation becomes $v'+(1-n)P(x)v=(1-n)Q(x)$, which is solved with an integrating factor.
cur.103.theory.1: The cases $n=0$ and $n=1$ are already linear and must not be transformed; $n=0$ is an ordinary linear nonhomogeneous equation and $n=1$ is separable. After solving for $v$, return with $y=v^{1/(1-n)}$ and fix the sign of the root from the initial condition.
cur.104.algorithm:
ay″ + by′ + cy = 0 と書く。
ar² + br + c = 0 を解く。
相異なる実根 r₁, r₂ に対して y = C₁e^{r₁x} + C₂e^{r₂x} を用いる。
初期条件を適用して C₁ と C₂ を求める。
方程式に代入して検証する。
cur.104.answer: 特性方程式は r² − 3r + 2 = 0 なので r = 1, 2、y = C₁eˣ + C₂e²ˣ。
cur.104.idea: 定数係数の同次方程式では y = e^{rx} を代入する。微分方程式は特性方程式 ar² + br + c = 0 になる。
cur.104.pitfall: 特性方程式の変数は y ではなく r である。y を代入し直してはならない。
cur.104.theory.0: Because the derivative of $e^{rx}$ is $re^{rx}$, substituting $y=e^{rx}$ turns every term into a coefficient times $e^{rx}$, and $e^{rx}$ factors out. Since $e^{rx}\neq 0$, what remains is the algebraic equation $ar^2+br+c=0$, whose roots determine the behaviour of the solution.
cur.104.theory.1: For distinct real roots $r_1\neq r_2$ there are two independent solutions $e^{r_1x}$ and $e^{r_2x}$, and the general solution is $y=C_1e^{r_1x}+C_2e^{r_2x}$. Their Wronskian is nonzero, so they really form a fundamental set. The signs of the roots decide whether the solution grows, decays or stays constant.
cur.105.algorithm:
特性方程式を解く。
r = α ± iβ なら α = −b/(2a)、β = √(4ac − b²)/(2a) を計算する。
y = e^{αx}(C₁ cos βx + C₂ sin βx) と書く。
初期条件を適用する。
代入して検証する。
cur.105.answer: r² + 1 = 0 より r = ±i、よって α = 0、β = 1、y = C₁ cos x + C₂ sin x。
cur.105.idea: 判別式が負のときは複素共役対 r = α ± iβ が得られる。オイラーの公式により、この対は指数関数と三角関数の積である実解になる。
cur.105.pitfall: α が 0 でないとき e^{αx} を落としてはいけない。振動はその指数関数を掛けたままである。
cur.105.theory.0: When $r=\alpha+i\beta$ is a root, $e^{(\alpha+i\beta)x}=e^{\alpha x}(\cos\beta x+i\sin\beta x)$ is a complex solution. Since the coefficients are real, the conjugate is also a solution, and a suitable linear combination gives the two real solutions $e^{\alpha x}\cos\beta x$ and $e^{\alpha x}\sin\beta x$.
cur.105.theory.1: The factor $e^{\alpha x}$ is the amplitude envelope. If $\alpha<0$ the oscillation decays, if $\alpha>0$ it grows, and if $\alpha=0$ it is pure oscillation. $\beta$ is the angular frequency and the period is $\frac{2\pi}{\beta}$. This is exactly the damped oscillator met in mechanical applications.
cur.106.algorithm:
特性方程式を解く。
r が重根なら y = (C₁ + C₂x)e^{rx} を用いる。
一般の線形方程式では y = v(x)y₁ と置く。
代入して v′ に関する1階方程式を得る。
2回積分し、初期条件を適用する。
cur.106.answer: r² + 4r + 4 = (r + 2)² なので r = −2 は重根、y = (C₁ + C₂x)e⁻²ˣ。
cur.106.idea: 特性根が重根のときは指数解が1つしか得られない。2つ目の独立解はそれに x を掛けるか、より一般には階数低減法で求める。
cur.106.pitfall: 重根は e^{rx} が2つ得られるわけではない。2つ目の解には因子 x が必要である。
cur.106.theory.0: If $r$ is a double root, $y_1=e^{rx}$ is one solution but a second copy of $e^{rx}$ is not independent. For a second-order constant-coefficient equation the second solution is $y_2=xe^{rx}$, and the general solution is $y=(C_1+C_2x)e^{rx}$.
cur.106.theory.1: The reason is reduction of order: setting $y=u(x)e^{rx}$ and substituting removes the $u$ term and leaves an equation for $u'$ whose solution is $u=C_1+C_2x$. A repeated root usually marks the boundary between non-oscillatory decay and oscillation, as in the critically damped spring.
cur.107.algorithm:
同次方程式を解いて y_h を求める。
g(x) とそのすべての導関数の形で y_p を予想する。
予想が同次解と重なるなら x を掛ける。
y_p を代入し、同類項の係数を比較する。
y = y_h + y_p とおき、初期条件を適用する。
cur.107.answer: 同次解は C₁eˣ + C₂e²ˣ です。eˣ はすでに同次方程式の解なので、推定解は y_p = Axeˣ となります。代入すると A = −1 が得られ、y = C₁eˣ + C₂e²ˣ − xeˣ となります。
cur.107.idea: 未定係数法では、強制項と同じ形の特殊解を予想し、代入してその係数を定める。
cur.107.pitfall: 強制項が同次解と一致する場合、そのままの予想は失敗する。係数を比較する前に x を掛ける。
cur.107.theory.0: If the right side is a polynomial, an exponential, a sine or cosine, or a product of these, the particular solution has the same shape. For example $g(x)=e^{x}$ suggests $y_p=Ae^{x}$, and $g(x)=\cos 2x$ suggests $y_p=A\cos 2x+B\sin 2x$. Substituting and equating coefficients determines $A$ and $B$.
cur.107.theory.1: If the guessed term is itself a solution of the homogeneous equation, the plain guess fails because the left side becomes zero. Then multiply the guess by $x^s$, where $s$ is the multiplicity of that root in the characteristic equation. For a composite $g$, superposition lets you build a particular solution for each piece and add them.
cur.108.algorithm:
同次方程式の独立な解 y₁, y₂ を求める。
y = u₁y₁ + u₂y₂ と置く。
u₁′y₁ + u₂′y₂ = 0 と u₁′y₁′ + u₂′y₂′ = g を解く。
積分して u₁ と u₂ を求める。
同次解を加え、初期条件を適用する。
cur.108.answer: y₁ = cos x、y₂ = sin x とすると、連立方程式から u₁′ = −sin x sec x、u₂′ = cos x sec x。よって y = C₁ cos x + C₂ sin x + cos x ln|cos x| + x sin x。
cur.108.example: y″ + y = sec x を解く。
cur.108.idea: 定数変化法では、同次解の定数を関数に置き換える。未定係数法と違い、連続な強制項であればどれにも使える。
cur.108.pitfall: まず y″ の係数で割る。定数変化法の公式はその係数が 1 であることを前提とする。
cur.108.theory.0: Setting $y=u_1y_1+u_2y_2$ and imposing $u_1'y_1+u_2'y_2=0$ simplifies the derivatives and gives the system $\begin{cases}u_1'y_1+u_2'y_2=0\\ u_1'y_1'+u_2'y_2'=g\end{cases}$. Solving it with the Wronskian $W=y_1y_2'-y_1'y_2$ gives $u_1'=-\frac{y_2g}{W}$ and $u_2'=\frac{y_1g}{W}$.
cur.108.theory.1: After integrating, the particular solution is $y_p=u_1y_1+u_2y_2$. This method is the only analytic route for $g$ such as $\sec x$ or $\ln x$, which have no simple guessed shape. The requirements are that the coefficient of $y''$ equals 1 and that the Wronskian is nonzero on the interval.
cur.109.algorithm:
特性多項式を書く。
すべての根とその重複度を求める。
重複度 m の実根 r に対して e^{rx}, xe^{rx}, …, x^{m−1}e^{rx} を含める。
重複度 m の複素対 α ± iβ に対して、k = 0, …, m−1 について e^{αx}x^k cos βx と e^{αx}x^k sin βx を含める。
項をまとめ、初期条件を適用する。
cur.109.answer: 特性多項式は (r − 1)³ なので y = (C₁ + C₂x + C₃x²)eˣ。
cur.109.idea: 定数係数の高階同次方程式では、特性多項式がすべての解を与える。実根は指数関数を、複素根は振動を与え、重複度は x のべきを加える。
cur.109.pitfall: 重複度 m の根には m 個の独立解が必要である。指数関数1つで止めてはいけない。
cur.109.theory.0: A characteristic polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ roots counted with multiplicity. Each real root $r$ of multiplicity $m$ gives the solutions $e^{rx}, xe^{rx},\ldots,x^{m-1}e^{rx}$. Each complex pair $\alpha\pm i\beta$ of multiplicity $m$ gives $x^ke^{\alpha x}\cos\beta x$ and $x^ke^{\alpha x}\sin\beta x$ for $k=0..m-1$.
cur.109.theory.1: Together these solutions form a fundamental set, and the general solution is their linear combination. Because the coefficients are constant, the roots can be found by factoring or numerically. The shape of the roots determines the qualitative behaviour: growth, decay or oscillation.
cur.110.algorithm:
同次解を求める。
g とそのすべての導関数の形で y_p を予想する。
予想が同次解と重なるとき x^s を掛ける。ここで s は強制項の根の重複度である。
代入して係数を比較する。
y_h と y_p を加え、初期条件を適用する。
cur.110.answer: 同次方程式の根は 0（2重）と 1 なので y_h = C₁ + C₂x + C₃eˣ。予想 y_p = Axeˣ から A = 1、よって y = C₁ + C₂x + C₃eˣ + xeˣ。
cur.110.idea: 未定係数法の予想は任意の階数に拡張できる。強制項が和なら、各項について特殊解を1つずつ求めて加える。
cur.110.pitfall: 掛ける因子は x^s であり、s は特性多項式における強制項の根の重複度である。
cur.110.theory.0: For an $n$th-order equation with forcing $g$, if $g$ is a combination of polynomials, exponentials and trigonometric terms, the particular solution has the same shape. If a piece of $g$ overlaps a characteristic root, the guess for that piece is multiplied by $x^s$, where $s$ is the multiplicity of that root.
cur.110.theory.1: Superposition says that for $g=g_1+g_2$, if $y_{p1}$ solves $g_1$ and $y_{p2}$ solves $g_2$, then $y_{p1}+y_{p2}$ solves $g$. This splits the guess into smaller problems and avoids one large, error-prone guess.
cur.66.algorithm:
最高階の導関数を特定する。それが階数である。
y を含む項をすべて左辺に、強制項を右辺に移す。
各 y の項が x の係数と y または y の導関数の積であることを確かめる。
y のべき、積、非線形関数が現れれば、方程式は非線形である。
解法を選ぶ前に、階数・線形性・同次性を記録する。
cur.66.answer: 1つ目は2階の線形非同次方程式である。2つ目は y が2乗で現れるため1階の非線形方程式である。
cur.66.example: y″ + 3y′ + 2y = eˣ と y′ = y² を分類する。
cur.66.idea: 線形方程式では y とその導関数は1次のみで現れ、係数は x のみに依存する。y·y′ のような積や sin y のような非線形関数があれば、方程式は非線形になる。
cur.66.pitfall: 階数と次数は異なる。1階方程式でも非線形になり得るし、y·y′ は各因子が線形でも非線形である。
cur.66.theory.0: An $n$th-order linear equation can be written $a_n(x)y^{(n)}+\cdots+a_0(x)y=g(x)$. Two facts matter for this family: the general solution carries as many constants as the order, and superposition holds. Superposition says that if $y_1$ and $y_2$ solve the homogeneous equation, so does every linear combination.
cur.66.theory.1: Nonlinearity is not always bad, but the linear methods do not apply. Terms such as $y^2$, $y\,y'$, $\sin y$ or a coefficient depending on $y$ make the equation nonlinear. An equation can be first order and still nonlinear; the two properties are independent.
cur.67.algorithm:
初期値問題 y′ = f(x,y)、y(x₀) = y₀ を書く。
f が (x₀,y₀) の周りの長方形上で連続であることを確かめる。そうすれば解は存在する。
そこで ∂f/∂y が連続であることを確かめる。そうすれば解は一意である。
一意性を用いて解曲線の交差を排除する。
判定が成り立たなければ、複数の解や特異解を探す。
cur.67.answer: f = y² と ∂f/∂y = 2y はともに (0,1) の近くで連続なので、解は一意である。解くと −∞ < x < 1 で y = 1/(1 − x)。
cur.67.example: y′ = y²、y(0) = 1 は一意な解をもつか。
cur.67.idea: 初期値問題は与えられた点を通る解を求める。f の連続性は存在を保証し、y に関するリプシッツ条件は一意性を保証する。
cur.67.pitfall: f の連続性は存在のみを与える。一意性には f が y に関してどれだけ速く変化するかの評価も必要である。
cur.67.theory.0: The existence and uniqueness theorem says that if $f$ and $\partial f/\partial y$ are continuous on a rectangle around $(x_0,y_0)$, then $y'=f(x,y)$ with $y(x_0)=y_0$ has a unique solution on some interval containing $x_0$. Continuity of $f$ gives existence, and a bounded $\partial f/\partial y$ gives uniqueness.
cur.67.theory.1: The condition is sufficient, not necessary. If the test fails a unique solution may still exist; for example $f=y^{1/3}$ is continuous at $y=0$ but its derivative is unbounded there. For linear problems, continuity of the coefficients on an interval is enough for existence and uniqueness.
cur.68.algorithm:
y_{n+1} = f(n, y_n) と書き、y₀ を記録する。
最初の数項を計算して規則性を見る。
y_{n+1} = a y_n + b に対して不動点 y* = b/(1 − a) を解く。
y_n = y* + (y₀ − y*)aⁿ と書く。
安定性を確かめる: |a| < 1 なら収束し、|a| > 1 なら発散する。
cur.68.answer: 不動点は y* = 6 なので y_n = 6 − 5(0.5)ⁿ。|0.5| < 1 なので数列は 6 に収束する。
cur.68.example: y₀ = 1 として y_{n+1} = 0.5y_n + 3 を解く。
cur.68.idea: 1階差分方程式は、1つの整数ステップから次へ進む。線形方程式には不動点があり、倍率のべきによる明示的な公式が存在する。
cur.68.pitfall: 添字 n は離散的である。n について微分したり積分したりしてはいけない。
cur.68.theory.0: The fixed point $y^*$ is where the sequence stops changing: $y^*=ay^*+b$, so $y^*=\frac{b}{1-a}$ for $a\neq 1$. Writing $y_n=y^*+(y_0-y^*)\,a^n$ shows that the distance from the fixed point is multiplied by $a$ at each step.
cur.68.theory.1: If $|a|<1$ then $a^n\to 0$ and the sequence converges to $y^*$ (stable). If $|a|>1$ it diverges, and if $a=-1$ it oscillates between two values. The index $n$ is discrete; differentiation and integration with respect to it make no sense, and the tools are summation and iteration.
cur.69.algorithm:
強制項を F₀ cos ωt として方程式を標準形に書く。
同次（過渡）解を求める。
振動数 ω の特殊解を予想する。
その振幅と位相を求める。
2つの部分を加え、ω が固有振動数に等しいときの共振を特定する。
cur.69.answer: 同次部分は C₁ cos ω₀t + C₂ sin ω₀t。特殊解は F₀ cos ωt/(ω₀² − ω²) であり、全体の応答はこれらの和である。
cur.69.example: ω ≠ ω₀ として y″ + ω₀²y = F₀ cos ωt を解く。
cur.69.idea: 正弦的な強制を受けるばね-質量系は、過渡的な同次部分と、強制振動数での定常応答をもつ。2つの振動数が一致すると共振が起こる。
cur.69.pitfall: 共振では分母が 0 になる。そのとき特殊解は t sin ω₀t を含み、いくらでも大きくなる。
cur.69.theory.0: The equation $my''+cy'+ky=F_0\cos\omega t$ has two parts. The homogeneous solution decays when there is damping and disappears after a while; the particular solution oscillates at the frequency $\omega$ and persists. The steady-state amplitude is proportional to $1/\sqrt{(k-m\omega^2)^2+(c\omega)^2}$.
cur.69.theory.1: The natural frequency is $\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}$. As $\omega$ approaches $\omega_0$ the denominator shrinks and the amplitude grows. With no damping and $\omega=\omega_0$, the particular solution takes the form $t\sin\omega_0t$ and the amplitude grows without bound; this is resonance. With damping the amplitude becomes large but stays finite.
cur.70.algorithm:
y⁽ⁿ⁾ の係数を 1 として方程式を書く。
係数と g が区間上で連続であることを確かめる。
n 個の独立な同次解を求める。
強制項に対する特殊解を加える。
n 個の初期条件を適用してすべての定数を定める。
cur.70.answer: r³ − 1 = (r − 1)(r² + r + 1) なので、根は 1 と −1/2 ± i√3/2。一般解は eˣ と e^{−x/2} cos(√3x/2)、e^{−x/2} sin(√3x/2) を組み合わせたものである。
cur.70.idea: n 階線形方程式の解空間は n 次元である。区間上での係数の連続性は、n 個の初期条件に対する一意な解を保証する。
cur.70.pitfall: n 階方程式には n 個の独立解と n 個の初期条件が必要である。階数ごとに定数が1つである。
cur.70.theory.0: For $y^{(n)}+p_{n-1}(x)y^{(n-1)}+\cdots+p_0(x)y=g(x)$, if the coefficients and $g$ are continuous on an interval $I$, the initial value problem with $n$ conditions at one point has a unique solution on $I$. A set of $n$ independent solutions is called a fundamental set, and its Wronskian is nonzero on $I$.
cur.70.theory.1: The general solution is the linear combination $y=C_1y_1+\cdots+C_ny_n$ plus one particular solution. For constant coefficients, the characteristic polynomial of degree $n$ determines everything, and each root contributes as many solutions as its multiplicity.
cur.71.algorithm:
n 個の独立な同次解 y₁, …, y_n を求める。
ロンスキアン W を計算する。
連立方程式 Σu_k′y_k = 0, …, Σu_k′y_k^{(n−2)} = 0, Σu_k′y_k^{(n−1)} = g を解く。
積分して u₁, …, u_n を求める。
y = y_h + Σu_k y_k とおき、初期条件を適用する。
cur.71.answer: 同次解は 1, eˣ, e⁻ˣ である。定数変化法により特殊解 −x が得られ、y = C₁ + C₂eˣ + C₃e⁻ˣ − x。
cur.71.idea: 高階の定数変化法では、ロンスキアンを用いて n 個の未知関数の導関数を求める。それらを積分して特殊解を構成する。
cur.71.pitfall: ロンスキアンは区間上で 0 でない必要がある。そうでなければ選んだ解は従属で、連立方程式は一意な解をもたない。
cur.71.theory.0: For an $n$th-order equation, write the particular solution as $y_p=\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_i(x)y_i(x)$ and impose $n-1$ extra conditions so the derivatives simplify. The resulting system is $\sum_i u_i'y_i^{(k)}=0$ for $k=0..n-2$ and $\sum_i u_i'y_i^{(n-1)}=g$.
cur.71.theory.1: Solving this system with the Wronskian $W$ gives $u_i'=\frac{W_i}{W}$, where $W_i$ is the determinant with column $i$ replaced by the right-hand side. After integrating, the particular solution is obtained. The Wronskian must be nonzero on the interval so that the $y_i$ are independent.
cur.98.algorithm:
方程式を y′ = f(x, y) と書く。
x と y の格子を選び、各点で f を評価する。
各格子点に傾き f の短い線分を描く。
線分に沿う解曲線を描き、f = 0 となる点を印す。
長期的な振る舞いを方向場から読み取る。数値解法で確認できる。
cur.98.answer: 傾きは y = 0 と y = 2 で 0 である。2直線の間の解は y = 2 に向かって増加し、y = 2 より上の解はそこへ減少するので、y = 2 は安定である。
cur.98.example: y′ = y(2 − y) の方向場を描く。
cur.98.idea: 方向場は、格子点における傾き y′ = f(x,y) を描いたものである。解曲線は線分に接するので、公式を求める前に増加・減少・平衡が分かる。
cur.98.pitfall: 方向場は振る舞いの示唆を与えるが証明ではない。特異解や、描画範囲外での符号の変化を見落とすことがある。
cur.98.theory.0: A direction field turns a differential equation into a picture. Each segment shows only a slope, not a value, so solutions are read from the field rather than computed from it. Curves that are tangent to the segments at every point are called integral curves.
cur.98.theory.1: If $f$ and $\partial f/\partial y$ are continuous, two integral curves can never cross; two solutions passing through one point would violate uniqueness. The lines where $f=0$ are equilibrium solutions and usually separate the directions of motion.
cur.99.algorithm:
方程式を標準形 y′ + P(x)y = Q(x) に書く。
μ = exp(∫P(x) dx) を計算する。
各項に μ を掛ける。
左辺を (μy)′ と書き換え、両辺を積分する。
y について解き、初期条件があれば適用する。
cur.99.answer: ここでは P = 1/x なので μ = x。すると (xy)′ = x³、xy = x⁴/4 + C、よって y = x³/4 + C/x。
cur.99.example: x > 0 で y′ + y/x = x² を解く。
cur.99.idea: 1階線形方程式は、積分因子 μ(x) を掛けることで完全形にできる。左辺は μy の導関数になるので、1回の積分で解が得られる。
cur.99.pitfall: P を読み取る前に y′ の係数で割る。そうしないと積分因子が誤りになる。
cur.99.theory.0: The integrating factor comes from the product rule. We want to write $\mu y'+\mu P y$ as $(\mu y)'$. Expanding $(\mu y)'=\mu y'+\mu'y$ shows that $\mu'=\mu P$, that is $\mu=e^{\int P\,dx}$.
cur.99.theory.1: After multiplying, the equation becomes $(\mu y)'=\mu Q$ and only two integrals remain. The interval of validity is the largest interval on which $P$, $Q$ and $\mu$ are continuous and the coefficient of $y'$ does not vanish.

ode.a1: Linear independence is checked on an interval where the functions and W are defined and continuous.
ode.a2: The envelope is defined where F and F_c are smooth and eliminating c is valid.
ode.a3: F is smooth and the family slope is finite where the trajectories are computed; c was eliminated before solving.
ode.c12: RK4 with automatic step subdivision; the plot marks the computed trajectories.
ode.c14: The symbolic W matches the numeric determinant at sampled points.
ode.c17: Envelope is tangent to the family
ode.c18: The implicit slopes of the envelope and of the family agree at the contact point.
ode.c_exact_fail: The symbolic relation was not verified; branch points may exist.
ode.c_exact_ok: du is proportional to M dx + N dy; the solution family is valid.
ode.c_implicit_ok: The implicit relation satisfies y′ = p(y).
ode.c_substitution_fail: Symbolic verification was inconclusive; check the domain.
ode.c_substitution_ok: Differentiating the answer satisfies the equation.
ode.n.autonomous_quadratic: 方程式には x も y も明示的に含まれません。p = y′、q = y″ と置くと q についての二次方程式が残ります。各根 q(p) を dx = dp/q、dy = p·dp/q として分離すると、パラメータ解 (x(p), y(p)) が得られます。
ode.n.clairaut_form: The equation has the Clairaut form y = xp + f(p) with p = y′; f(p) = {f}.
ode.n.cofactor_expansion: Cofactor expansion along the first row.
ode.n.differential_form: M dx + N dy = 0 with M = {M} and N = {N}.
ode.n.differential_form_not_exact: M dx + N dy = 0 is not exact; rewriting it as y' = -M/N.
ode.n.eliminate_c_direct: Form the system F = 0 and F_x + F_y·y′ = 0. Differentiating and simplifying removes c, so the derivative equation is already the family ODE.
ode.n.eliminate_c_value: Form the system F = 0 and F_x + F_y·y′ = 0. From F = 0, c = {c}; substituting this into the derivative equation removes c and gives the family ODE.
ode.n.family_parameter_c: F(x,y,c) = 0, where c is the parameter.
ode.n.forcing_ansatz: The forcing term splits into e^(kx), polynomial and sine/cosine pieces. Because k + i b has multiplicity {mult} as a characteristic root, the ansatz is {ansatz}.
ode.n.horizontal_family: The family slope is 0, so the family is horizontal and the trajectory family is the vertical lines x = C.
ode.n.infinite_trajectory_slope: The trajectory slope is infinite, so the family consists of the vertical lines x = C.

ode.n10: The right side is quadratic in y, so this is Riccati: y′ = P y² + Q y + R with P = {n0}, Q = {n1} and R = {n2}.
ode.n11: Verified by substitution into the equation.
ode.n12: With y = y₁ + 1/z and one known particular solution, the nonlinear equation becomes the linear equation z′ + (2P·y₁ + Q)z = −P.
ode.n13: With y = −u′/(P u), the equation becomes u″ − (Q + P′/P)u′ + P R u = 0.
ode.n14: The solution u is obtained, then y = −u′/(P u) returns the Riccati solution.
ode.n15: This is the Bernoulli form y′ + P(x)y = Q(x)y^n with n = {n0}, P = {n1} and Q = {n2}.
ode.n16: With v = y^(1−n) the equation becomes linear: v′ + {n0}v = {n1}.
ode.n17: The linear equation is solved with an integrating factor to obtain v(x).
ode.n18: Because 1−n is even, solving explicitly for y would drop one branch; the complete family is kept in implicit form.
ode.n19: The substitution y = v^(1/(1−n)) returns to the original variable.
ode.n2: Differentiating both sides and using y′ = p gives (x + f′(p))·dp/dx = 0.
ode.n20: After rearrangement: y′ + P(x)y = Q(x) with P = {n0} and Q = {n1}.
ode.n21: μ = exp(∫P dx); multiplying by μ turns both sides into (μy)′ = μQ.
ode.n22: Integrating gives ∫μQ dx = {n0}; dividing by μ isolates y and leaves C free.
ode.n23: Replacing y by v·x leaves an expression that depends on v alone, so the equation is homogeneous: it depends only on the ratio y/x.
ode.n24: With y = v·x the product rule gives y′ = v + x·v′, so the equation becomes x·v′ = F(v) − v.
ode.n25: Here F(v) = v, giving the line family y = Cx.
ode.n26: The transformed equation is separable: dv/(F(v) − v) = dx/x.
ode.n27: Both sides are integrated and share a single constant.
ode.n28: Substituting v = y/x returns to the original variable and gives the implicit solution.
ode.n29: The right side factors as f(x) = {n0} and g(y) = {n1}, so the equation is separable.
ode.n3: The first factor dp/dx = 0 gives p = C, hence the line family y = Cx + f(C).
ode.n30: Dividing by g(y) gives dy/g(y) = f(x) dx; each side now has one variable only.
ode.n31: Integrating each side with respect to its own variable, with one shared constant C, gives the implicit solution.
ode.n32: The right side is built from the linear combination ax + by alone, so a single substitution turns it separable.
ode.n33: With u = a·x + y we get u′ = a + y′, so the equation becomes u′ = a + f(u), which is separable.
ode.n34: Both sides are integrated, keeping a single shared constant.
ode.n35: Restoring u = a·x + y gives the solution of the original equation.
ode.n36: ∂M/∂y = {n0} and ∂N/∂x = {n1}; they agree, so the equation is exact and a potential u exists with ∂u/∂x = M and ∂u/∂y = N.
ode.n37: Integrate M with respect to x (the constant is φ(y)); comparing ∂u/∂y with N gives φ′(y) = {n0} and φ(y) = {n1}.
ode.n38: The level curves of the potential are the solutions, so u(x,y) = C.
ode.n39: ∂M/∂y = {n0} and ∂N/∂x = {n1}; they differ, so the original equation is not exact and needs an integrating factor.
ode.n4: Since f′(p) = 0, the condition x + f′(p) = 0 gives no finite p; there is no singular solution.
ode.n41: Multiplying by μ makes the equation exact; integrating the first term with respect to x (constant φ(y)) and comparing ∂u/∂y with the second term gives φ′(y) = {n0} and φ(y) = {n1}.
ode.n42: The solution family is the level curves of this potential: u(x,y) = C.
ode.n44: A linear combination of the basis functions with arbitrary constants.
ode.n45: Only the order-{n0} derivative and a function of x occur, so the equation can be integrated {n1} times directly.
ode.n46: Integrating lowers the order by one and introduces the constant {n0}.
ode.n47: No term contains y itself, only x and derivatives of y up to order {n0}. This is an equation missing the dependent variable.
ode.n48: Set {n0} = y′. Then y″ = {n1}′, y‴ = {n2}″, and in general y^(k) = {n3}^(k−1); the order drops by one and the equation is written in {n4} and x.
ode.n49: In the following steps {n0} is the dependent variable and x is the independent variable; wherever the generic text says y, it means {n1} here.
ode.n5: The second factor x + f′(p) = 0 gives x = {n0} and y = f(p) − p f′(p) = {n1}; eliminating p with p = {n2} gives the envelope.
ode.n50: {n0} could not be isolated explicitly; the same relation is written with {n1} = y′ restored.
ode.n51: Since {n0} = y′, one more integration gives y and introduces the constant C{n1}.
ode.n52: The independent variable x does not appear explicitly; the equation is missing the independent variable.
ode.n53: Set {n0} = y′(x) and treat {n1} as a function of y. By the chain rule y″ = d{n2}/dx = (d{n3}/dy)(dy/dx) = {n4}·d{n5}/dy, so the equation becomes a first-order equation in {n6}(y).
ode.n54: In the following steps y is the independent variable and {n0} is the dependent variable; wherever the generic text says x it means y, and wherever it says y it means {n1}.
ode.n55: {n0} could not be isolated explicitly; the relation is written with {n1} = y′ restored.
ode.n56: The first-order equation gives {n0} as a function of y.
ode.n57: Writing y′ = {n0}(y) gives dy/{n1}(y) = dx. Integrate the left side in y and the right side in x; the integration constant C2 appears.

ode.n8: With the integrating factor μ = {n0}, x(p) is obtained.

study.derivative.key_idea.0: Average rate of change is a secant slope; the derivative is the limit as the two points merge.
study.derivative.key_idea.1: Power, product, quotient and chain rules turn the limit definition into fast algebra.
study.derivative.key_idea.2: A derivative is a function in its own right: f′ can be differentiated again to get f″.
study.derivative.key_idea.3: Implicit differentiation handles curves written as F(x, y) = 0, not just y = f(x).
study.derivative.key_idea.4: The sign of f′ gives increasing/decreasing behaviour; the sign of f″ gives concavity.
study.derivative.pitfalls: The usual mistakes are forgetting the chain rule inside a composite function and treating the derivative as an average slope. A derivative is local: it depends on the behaviour arbitrarily close to the point.
study.derivative.short_answer: The derivative is the instantaneous rate of change of a function. It is the limit of the difference quotient and equals the slope of the tangent line at that point.
study.derivative.subtitle: Instantaneous rate of change, the tangent line and the rules that make differentiation mechanical.
study.derivative.theory.0: A precise definition grows out of a simple idea. To get the slope of a curve at $x_0$, take two nearby points and compute the slope of the secant line. As the gap $h$ shrinks to zero, that slope tends to the tangent slope: $f'(x_0)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x_0+h)-f(x_0)}{h}$. If this limit exists and is finite, the function is differentiable there. Differentiability is stronger than continuity: every differentiable function is continuous, but not conversely (take $|x|$ at zero).
study.derivative.theory.1: We do not have to take a limit every time. A few rules do all the work: the power rule $\frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1}$, the product rule $\frac{d}{dx}(fg)=f'g+fg'$, the quotient rule $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{f}{g}=\frac{f'g-fg'}{g^2}$, and above all the chain rule $\frac{d}{dx}f(g(x))=f'(g(x))\,g'(x)$. Any function built from sums, products, quotients and compositions differentiates with these four rules.
study.derivative.theory.2: The derivative is written $f'(x)$, $y'$ or $\frac{dy}{dx}$. Because it is a function, it can be differentiated again: $f''$ or $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$. For motion on a line, if $s(t)$ is position then $s'(t)$ is velocity and $s''(t)$ is acceleration; the same reading returns when second-order differential equations are modelled.
study.derivative.theory.3: Near $x=a$ every differentiable curve looks like its tangent. That observation gives the linear approximation $f(x)\approx f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)$. The error is of order $(x-a)^2$, which is why the approximation is excellent for small changes. This is also the idea behind linearisation and Euler's method for solving differential equations numerically.
study.derivative.theory.4: The sign of the derivative reveals the behaviour: $f'>0$ means increasing, $f'<0$ decreasing, and $f'=0$ marks a critical point. The second derivative shows concavity; $f''>0$ curves upward and $f''<0$ curves downward. The mean value theorem guarantees that on an interval where the function is continuous and differentiable inside, some point has instantaneous slope equal to the average slope across the interval.
study.derivative.theory.5: Sometimes a curve is not given explicitly as $y=f(x)$ but implicitly by $F(x,y)=0$. Then we differentiate both sides with respect to $x$ and solve for $y'$ as the unknown; this is implicit differentiation. For circles and ellipses, where solving for $y$ is awkward, it is the only practical way to get the slope.

study.integral.key_idea.0: A Riemann sum approximates area with rectangles; the integral is the limit as the rectangles get thin.
study.integral.key_idea.1: An antiderivative reverses differentiation, so every derivative rule has an integral counterpart.
study.integral.key_idea.2: Substitution reverses the chain rule; integration by parts reverses the product rule.
study.integral.key_idea.3: Area below the axis counts as negative, which is why the integral is called signed area.
study.integral.key_idea.4: Improper integrals take a limit at an infinite endpoint or a singularity.
study.integral.pitfalls: Do not drop the constant of integration in an indefinite integral, and do not forget to change the limits when you use substitution. A definite integral can be negative even when the geometric area is positive.
study.integral.short_answer: The definite integral is the signed area between a curve and the x-axis. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says that integrating a rate recovers the total change.
study.integral.subtitle: Signed area, the Riemann sum and the Fundamental Theorem that links integration to differentiation.
study.integral.theory.0: The area under a graph is approximated by thin rectangles. Split the interval into $n$ pieces and sample one point in each; the Riemann sum is $\sum_{k=1}^{n} f(x_k^*)\Delta x$. As $n\to\infty$ and $\Delta x\to 0$ this sum approaches a number called the definite integral: $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n} f(x_k^*)\Delta x$.
study.integral.theory.1: The fundamental theorem has two halves. The first says the accumulation function $A(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ has derivative $f(x)$; integration and differentiation are inverse operators. The second makes computation practical: if $F$ is any antiderivative, $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)$. That is why the table of antiderivatives is the derivative table read backwards.
study.integral.theory.2: Two techniques reverse the two big derivative rules. Substitution reverses the chain rule: with $u=g(x)$, $\int f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx=\int f(u)\,du$. Integration by parts reverses the product rule: $\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$. Choosing $u$ and $dv$ is most of the work; the LIATE rule of thumb suggests algebraic factors for $u$ and exponential or trigonometric factors for $dv$.
study.integral.theory.3: A definite integral is a number, not a family of functions, so no constant $C$ appears. Swapping the limits changes the sign, and regions below the $x$-axis count as negative. That is why it is called signed area rather than geometric area.
study.integral.theory.4: If the interval is unbounded or the function blows up at a point, the integral is improper and defined by a limit. For example $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$ converges only for $p>1$, while $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x}\,dx$ diverges. Both integrands tend to zero; how fast they tend to zero decides convergence, not the mere fact that they do.

study.ode_applications.pitfalls: Keep the units consistent and check that the answer is physically sensible. A negative temperature or a population above the carrying capacity signals an algebra or sign error, not a new phenomenon.
study.ode_applications.short_answer: A differential equation models how a quantity changes. The solution predicts the future state from an initial condition, and the constants in the model come from the physical data.
study.ode_applications.subtitle: Turn a physical statement into an equation, solve it, then read the prediction back in the original units.
study.ode_applications.theory.0: Before any algebra, decide what is conserved: mass, energy, heat or momentum. The rate of change of a quantity equals what comes in minus what goes out. Simplifying assumptions (perfect mixing, drag proportional to speed, constant ambient temperature) must be stated explicitly, because the validity of the answer depends on them.
study.ode_applications.theory.1: The simplest model is exponential growth or decay: $\frac{dy}{dt}=ky$, with solution $y(t)=y_0e^{kt}$. For $k>0$ the quantity grows, for $k<0$ it decays, and the doubling time is $\frac{\ln 2}{k}$. The model holds only while resources are unlimited; real populations bend away as limits appear.
study.ode_applications.theory.2: Newton's law of cooling says the rate of change of temperature is proportional to the difference from the surroundings: $\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-T_m)$. The solution $T(t)=T_m+(T_0-T_m)e^{-kt}$ approaches the ambient temperature exponentially, never crossing it. A well-mixed tank has the same structure, with $Q(t)$ the mass of dissolved substance.
study.ode_applications.theory.3: A mechanical oscillator is written with $m\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}$ and damping with $\gamma\frac{dy}{dt}$: $m\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}+\gamma\frac{dy}{dt}+ky=F(t)$. The natural frequency is $\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}$. When the forcing frequency matches it, the amplitude grows without bound in the undamped model; that is resonance. The series LRC circuit obeys exactly the same equation with $L$, $R$ and $1/C$, so mechanical intuition carries over to electricity.
study.ode_applications.theory.4: Logistic growth adds a carrying capacity: $\frac{dP}{dt}=rP\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)$. It is nearly exponential for small populations, slows near $K$, and produces the S-curve. The equilibrium $P=K$ is stable, because for $P>K$ the derivative is negative and pushes the population back.

study.ode_types.key_idea.0: Order is the highest derivative present; it is the number of constants in the general solution.
study.ode_types.key_idea.1: Linear means y and its derivatives appear to the first power with coefficients depending only on x.
study.ode_types.key_idea.2: Homogeneous means g(x) = 0; nonhomogeneous equations add a particular solution to the homogeneous one.
study.ode_types.key_idea.3: An initial value problem fixes y and enough derivatives at one point; a boundary value problem fixes values at two points.
study.ode_types.key_idea.4: First-order standard forms include separable, linear, exact, Bernoulli and homogeneous equations.
study.ode_types.pitfalls: Order is not the same as degree. A nonlinear term such as y·y′ or sin(y) immediately makes the equation nonlinear. For a nonhomogeneous equation, never forget the particular solution.
study.ode_types.short_answer: A differential equation relates an unknown function to its derivatives. It is classified by order (highest derivative), by linearity, and by whether the right side is zero.
study.ode_types.subtitle: 階数、線形性、同次性、および一階の標準形を、講義で使う用語とともに扱います。
study.ode_types.theory.0: A solution of a differential equation is a function, not a number. The function $y=\phi(x)$ solves the equation on an interval $I$ if substitution makes the equation true on all of $I$. The general solution contains as many arbitrary constants as the order, and each particular solution is selected by an initial or boundary condition.
study.ode_types.theory.1: Order is the highest derivative present. An equation is linear when it can be written $a_n(x)y^{(n)}+\cdots+a_1(x)y'+a_0(x)y=g(x)$, so that $y$ and its derivatives appear only to the first power with coefficients depending on $x$ alone. If $g(x)=0$ the equation is homogeneous, otherwise nonhomogeneous. Linear equations obey superposition: a linear combination of solutions is again a solution.
study.ode_types.theory.2: First-order equations come in a small set of families. Separable: $y'=f(x)g(y)$. Linear: $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)$. Exact: $M(x,y)\,dx+N(x,y)\,dy=0$ with $M_y=N_x$. Homogeneous: $y'=f(y/x)$. Bernoulli: $y'+P(x)y=Q(x)y^n$. Each family has its own substitution or integrating factor; identifying the family is half of the solution.
study.ode_types.theory.3: An initial value problem adds the value of the function and enough derivatives at one point. The existence and uniqueness theorem says that if $f$ and $\partial f/\partial y$ are continuous on a rectangle around the initial point, a unique solution exists. The condition is sufficient, not necessary: failing the test does not prove that uniqueness fails. In a boundary value problem the conditions sit at two different points, and there may be no solution, one solution, or infinitely many.
study.ode_types.theory.4: For second and higher order equations, a homogeneous equation with constant coefficients becomes a characteristic equation. Distinct real roots give a combination of exponentials, complex roots bring sine and cosine, and a repeated root adds a factor $x$. For a nonhomogeneous equation the general solution is the homogeneous solution plus one particular solution: $y=y_h+y_p$.
study.ode_types.theory.5: When the coefficients are not constant, other methods take over: power series about an ordinary point, the Frobenius method about a regular singular point, and the Laplace transform for initial value problems with step or impulse input. The shape of the equation and the type of conditions choose the method, not personal taste.

theorem.cauchy.hypothesis.0: Both f and g are continuous on [a, b].
theorem.cauchy.hypothesis.2: g'(x) ≠ 0 on (a, b), which also gives g(b) ≠ g(a).
theorem.cauchy.pitfall.0: Taking g(x) = x recovers the ordinary Mean Value Theorem.
theorem.cauchy.pitfall.1: The condition on g is what prevents division by zero in the conclusion.
theorem.cauchy.pitfall.2: Cauchy's theorem is the tool behind L'Hôpital's rule.
theorem.cauchy.statement: If f and g are continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), and g'(x) ≠ 0 on (a, b), then there exists c in (a, b) with f'(c)/g'(c) equal to (f(b) − f(a)) / (g(b) − g(a)).
theorem.cauchy.title: Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem
theorem.cauchy.why: It compares the two functions through a common parameter: each is a curve, and the theorem locates a point where their tangent directions match the overall change.
theorem.darboux.hypothesis.0: f is differentiable on the interval.
theorem.darboux.hypothesis.1: The value k lies between f'(a) and f'(b).
theorem.darboux.pitfall.0: The derivative need not be continuous, so the ordinary IVT does not apply to it directly.
theorem.darboux.statement: If f is differentiable on an interval, then f' has the intermediate value property there: it takes every value between any two of its values.
theorem.darboux.title: Darboux's theorem
theorem.darboux.why: Derivatives cannot jump, even though they need not be continuous; this is a surprising and useful rigidity property.
theorem.differentiable_implies_continuou: f(x) = |x| is continuous but not differentiable at 0.
A vertical tangent gives an infinite slope and therefore no derivative.
If f is differentiable at c, then f is continuous at c. The converse fails: continuity does not imply differentiability.
A finite slope forces the graph to close up into a single unbroken point, so a jump or a hole is impossible wherever a derivative exists.
theorem.differentiation_rules.hypothesis: Each rule needs the relevant derivatives to exist.
The inverse rule needs f'(a) ≠ 0 at the point.
theorem.differentiation_rules.pitfall.0: The derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives.
theorem.differentiation_rules.pitfall.1: The chain rule leaves the inner function intact as a factor.
theorem.differentiation_rules.pitfall.2: The inverse rule gives the reciprocal slope, not the inverse of the function value.
theorem.differentiation_rules.statement: Product, quotient, chain and inverse function rules, stated as the algebra that turns the derivatives of the pieces into the derivative of the whole.
theorem.differentiation_rules.title: The differentiation rules
theorem.differentiation_rules.why: Differentiation is linear plus a small set of structural rules; every derivative is built by combining them.
theorem.evt.hypothesis.0: The interval is closed and bounded.
theorem.evt.hypothesis.1: f is continuous on the whole interval.
theorem.evt.pitfall.0: Both assumptions matter: f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1] and f(x) = x on (0, 1) both fail.
theorem.evt.pitfall.1: It guarantees the extremes exist; finding them still needs the critical-point work.
theorem.evt.statement: If f is continuous on a closed bounded interval [a, b], then f attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on that interval.
theorem.evt.title: Extreme Value Theorem (Weierstrass)
theorem.evt.why: A continuous curve on a finite closed interval cannot escape to infinity or sneak past an endpoint, so it must reach its highest and lowest values.
theorem.fermat.hypothesis.0: c is an interior point of the domain.
theorem.fermat.hypothesis.1: f has a local extremum at c.
theorem.fermat.pitfall.0: The converse is false: f'(c) = 0 does not guarantee an extremum (consider f(x) = x³ at 0).
theorem.fermat.pitfall.1: The point must be interior; an endpoint can be an extremum without f' being zero.
theorem.fermat.statement: If f has a local maximum or minimum at an interior point c of its domain and f is differentiable there, then f'(c) = 0.
theorem.fermat.title: Fermat's theorem
theorem.fermat.why: At a smooth peak or trough the tangent flattens out, so the instantaneous rate of change must be zero.
theorem.first_derivative_test.hypothesis: c is a critical point of f.
f is continuous at c and differentiable on a punctured neighbourhood of it.
theorem.first_derivative_test.pitfall.0: The test needs a genuine sign change on both sides, not just f'(c) = 0.
theorem.first_derivative_test.pitfall.1: If f' does not change sign, the point is a stationary turning point rather than an extremum.
theorem.first_derivative_test.statement: At a critical point c: if f' changes from positive to negative, c is a local maximum; if it changes from negative to positive, c is a local minimum; if it keeps its sign, c is neither.
theorem.first_derivative_test.title: First derivative test
theorem.first_derivative_test.why: The function switches from climbing to falling exactly at a maximum and the reverse at a minimum, so the sign change is the decisive evidence.
theorem.inflection.hypothesis.0: f'' exists on a neighbourhood of c.
theorem.inflection.pitfall.0: f''(c) = 0 alone is not enough; an actual sign change is required.
theorem.inflection.pitfall.1: f(x) = x⁴ has f''(0) = 0 but no inflection at the origin.
theorem.inflection.statement: If f'' exists and changes sign at c, then (c, f(c)) is an inflection point and the concavity of f flips there.
theorem.inflection.title: Inflection point criterion
theorem.inflection.why: Concavity describes which way the curve bends; when the bending direction flips, the curve has an inflection point.
theorem.lhopital.hypothesis.0: The quotient is an indeterminate form 0/0 or ±∞/±∞ at a.
theorem.lhopital.hypothesis.1: f and g are differentiable near a, with g'(x) ≠ 0 there.
theorem.lhopital.hypothesis.2: The limit of f'/g' exists (or is infinite).
theorem.lhopital.pitfall.0: Never apply it before verifying the form really is indeterminate.
theorem.lhopital.pitfall.1: The rule applies to the quotient as a whole, not to products or sums term by term.
theorem.lhopital.pitfall.2: For 0·∞, ∞−∞, 1^∞, 0^0 and ∞^0, rewrite the expression into a 0/0 or ∞/∞ quotient first.
theorem.lhopital.pitfall.3: If the new limit is worse, stop: the rule gave no information.
theorem.lhopital.statement: If f and g are differentiable near a and both tend to 0 or both tend to ±∞ at a, and the limit of f'(x)/g'(x) exists, then the limit of f(x)/g(x) equals that same limit.
theorem.lhopital.title: ロピタルの定理
theorem.lhopital.why: Near the point the two functions are dominated by their linear behaviour, so comparing their slopes replaces comparing their values.
x is close enough to a for the error to be acceptable.
theorem.linear_approximation.pitfall.0: The approximation degrades quickly away from a.
theorem.linear_approximation.pitfall.1: It is only first order: the error grows like (x − a)².
theorem.linear_approximation.statement: If f is differentiable at a, then for x near a we have f(x) ≈ f(a) + f'(a)(x − a), and the error is small compared with (x − a).
theorem.linear_approximation.title: Linear approximation and the differential
theorem.linear_approximation.why: Zooming in far enough makes any smooth curve look like its tangent line, which is the practical meaning of the derivative.
theorem.monotonicity.hypothesis.0: f is continuous on the interval and differentiable on its interior.
theorem.monotonicity.hypothesis.1: The sign of f' is constant on the interval.
theorem.monotonicity.pitfall.0: The intervals of monotonicity are separated by the critical points of f.
theorem.monotonicity.pitfall.1: A single critical point does not by itself determine the sign on either side.
theorem.monotonicity.statement: If f'(x) > 0 on an interval then f is strictly increasing there; if f'(x) < 0 then f is strictly decreasing there.
theorem.monotonicity.title: Monotonicity test
theorem.monotonicity.why: A positive slope means the graph climbs as you move right, so the sign of the derivative reads directly as the direction of the function.
theorem.mvt.pitfall.0: Continuity is required on the CLOSED interval and differentiability on the OPEN one.
theorem.mvt.pitfall.1: The theorem promises existence; it does not tell you where until you solve for c.
theorem.mvt.pitfall.2: f(x) = |x| on [−1, 1] shows differentiability cannot be dropped.
theorem.mvt.statement: If f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then there exists at least one c in (a, b) such that f'(c) equals the secant slope (f(b) − f(a)) / (b − a).
theorem.mvt.title: Mean Value Theorem (Lagrange)
theorem.mvt.why: Somewhere the instantaneous rate of change must equal the average rate of change over the whole interval, so some tangent is parallel to the secant.
theorem.rolle.hypothesis.0: f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b].
theorem.rolle.hypothesis.1: f is differentiable on the open interval (a, b).
theorem.rolle.pitfall.0: Without f(a) = f(b) the conclusion can fail completely.
theorem.rolle.pitfall.1: Rolle is the special horizontal case of the Mean Value Theorem.
theorem.rolle.statement: If f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b), then there exists at least one c in (a, b) with f'(c) = 0.
theorem.rolle.title: ロルの定理
theorem.rolle.why: If the graph starts and ends at the same height, it must turn around somewhere inside and that turning point has a horizontal tangent.
theorem.second_derivative_test.hypothesi: f'' exists and is continuous near c.
theorem.second_derivative_test.pitfall.0: When f''(c) = 0 nothing is decided; fall back to the first derivative test.
theorem.second_derivative_test.pitfall.1: This test only applies at stationary points, not at endpoints.
theorem.second_derivative_test.statement: If f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) > 0 then c is a local minimum; if f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) < 0 then c is a local maximum. If f''(c) = 0 the test is inconclusive.
theorem.second_derivative_test.title: Second derivative test
theorem.second_derivative_test.why: Concavity is the tiebreaker: an upward-opening curve at a flat point is a valley, and a downward-opening one is a peak.
theorem.taylor.hypothesis.0: f has n + 1 continuous derivatives on the interval.
theorem.taylor.hypothesis.1: ξ lies strictly between a and x.
theorem.taylor.pitfall.0: The remainder gives an error bound, not the exact error.
theorem.taylor.pitfall.1: The point ξ is guaranteed to exist but is not identified.
theorem.taylor.statement: If f has n + 1 derivatives on an interval containing a and x, then f(x) equals its degree n Taylor polynomial at a plus a remainder involving f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾ at some point between a and x.
theorem.taylor.title: Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder
theorem.taylor.why: A smooth function is locally indistinguishable from a polynomial, and the remainder measures exactly how good that approximation is.
theorem.zero_derivative.hypothesis.0: The set is a single interval, not a union of separate pieces.
theorem.zero_derivative.hypothesis.1: f is differentiable with zero derivative throughout it.
theorem.zero_derivative.pitfall.0: On a disconnected domain the conclusion can fail piecewise.
theorem.zero_derivative.pitfall.1: This is what justifies writing one arbitrary constant in an indefinite integral.
theorem.zero_derivative.statement: If f'(x) = 0 for every x in an interval, then f is constant on that interval.
theorem.zero_derivative.title: Zero derivative implies constant
theorem.zero_derivative.why: Two functions with the same derivative differ by a constant, which is why an antiderivative always carries a + C.

ui.a_curve_crosses_the_family_at_the_con: A curve crosses the family at the constant angle α when tan α = (m_t − m)/(1 + m_t m). Solving for the trajectory slope gives m_t = (m + tan α)/(1 − m tan α), the differential equation of the oblique family.
ui.a_definite_integral_adds_up_signed_ar: A definite integral adds up signed area; an indefinite integral lists every antiderivative at once. The two are linked by the fundamental theorem.
ui.a_derivative_is_a_local_rate: A derivative is a local rate
ui.a_first_order_equation_describes_a_wh: A first-order equation describes a whole family of curves. Solving finds the relation that makes the equation true, with one constant C left free until an initial condition fixes it.
ui.a_function_is_continuous_at_a_point_w: A function is continuous at a point when it is defined there, its two-sided limit exists, and that limit equals the function value. All three must hold together.
A function is continuous at a point when the left limit and the right limit exist, are equal, and equal the value of the function.
ui.a_horizontal_family_has_slope_0_the_o: A horizontal family has slope 0; the oblique trajectory slope is tan α = 1.

ui.a_stationary_turning_point_such_as_x_: A stationary turning point such as x = 0 for x³ has f' = 0 but is neither a maximum nor a minimum.
